outcomes: A Go service can hand a TypeScript consumer a typed client, and a TypeScript service can hand a Go consumer one, generated from the contract the provider commits rather than from either language's source
A client project generates itself from committed files only, so Git holds no generated client and two changes to one contract conflict on nothing but the contract

Everything that decides an emitted byte — the contract, the configuration and the formatter that canonicalizes the output — is a declared cache-key entry or part of the client's identity, so a cache hit is never a stale render

A gate that already runs — lint, test, build, validate — rejects a tracked generated client and a newly handwritten first-party transport; the guard reads committed inputs only, so it builds nothing and renders nothing
nonGoals: Owning the language emitters, which stay in go.putnami.dev/api and @putnami/client next to the runtimes their output depends on
Removing the low-level client APIs tests and explicit external adapters use
Guessing whether an unmarked specification is first-party
Choosing where a generated client lands — the client project, or the provider's committed clientgen.json for an in-module target, does

requirements.text: Generation reads the provider's committed contract, schema/openapi.json, which the core resolves from the client's generatedFrom service, or the provider's own for an in-module target. It builds no provider and reads no file a build writes, and no task invokes another language's extension or the CLI.

The extension manifest produces zero diagnostics under the protocol's comprehensive validation, stays on the v3 task contract with a declaration on every task and exactly one owner per declared output, and the same predicates reject a forged ownership or effect declaration.

client-generate owns exactly the generated closure: client.gen.go for a Go client project, the src directory for a TypeScript one, or the directory an in-module target of the provider's committed clientgen.json names. Authored files beside it are never captured or restored, a cache restore recreates a deleted client, and the output is read by the client project's dependents, so the planner runs none of their jobs while it is rewritten.

An output directory the provider's configuration chooses is never claimed at a literal path a later configuration can move out from under: it is declared only through a pathFrom naming a port the task actually reports, or not at all.

Preparation packages the runtime and the framework Go emitter side by side and the TypeScript emitter is the Putnami-installed package shim run through the lock-resolved runtime, so no task needs a framework source checkout. The emitter is packaged, never linked: no compiled package imports go.putnami.dev/api.
Each task declares exactly the effects it has, a task is cacheable only when no declared effect is one a cache hit cannot reproduce, and a dishonest declaration is rejected by the shared validator.

The emitted TypeScript is canonicalized by Biome, so the resolved configuration, its overrides, its extends chain and the EditorConfig beside it are generation inputs, and so is the workspace root package.json, which decides how the TypeScript client depends on @putnami/client. Every one of them is a declared cache-key entry, an input that cannot be declared fails resolution, and both generators key on the committed contract and sidecar, never on a .gen file a build of the run writes.

No task rewrites an authored source: discovery, generation and verification write generated clients only. None declares mutatesSources, the project-scoped sources write, the authored-source write or the workspace-files effect, and none performs one.

Provider authority comes from the workspace project index and each project's committed contract; unindexed trees and fixtures cannot be providers, an unmarked contract requires explicit thirdParty mode in the committed clientgen.json, and an x-putnami-external-contract operation is no provider operation. A committed clientgen.json reads only its sidecar, and the check reads the committed sidecar and the committed clientgen.json, never a build's copy.

Every third-party configuration carries an entry in its project's clientgen.external.json naming its authority, adapter, exact normalized callsites, owner, contract tests and reason. An entry exempts only the matching path, transport, symbol and fingerprint, never a first-party marker, and its schema matches the strict parser field for field. Each project commits its own inventories; its directory names the project and no entry does. The older root layout, whose entries name their project, is never read.

A generated client whose contract declares a response cache policy or an SSE continuation requires the matching runtime capability when it loads, and a client runtime that does not implement it stops the load; regenerating cannot fix it, upgrading the runtime can.
An operation a client's generatedFrom omitOperations leaves out is absent from its generated client, and naming an operation the provider's contract does not declare fails generation.

A provider may declare its service identity and no first-party operation at all: every route owned by an external authority, or none served. The committed contract sidecar is that declaration, so the check reads it the same on a cold clone, names no client for it and requires nothing. Only a genuinely empty set qualifies: a contract with one declared operation, or one the check could not read, is not empty, and a consumer of an empty contract is told to classify its callsite.

Go AST and TypeScript lexical analysis inventory each production HTTP, Connect, SSE and WebSocket callsite across aliases and project-scoped endpoint configuration. Sources come only from indexed project trees in the Git candidate cut; comments, strings, tests and generated files do not trigger, and framework runtime authority is bound to exact callsite identities. A failing diagnostic names the service and the generated binding to call, or the client project to create: a failed job emits no report.

The check joins validate as a workspace-once command: one guard runs per session whatever the selection, and no project opts out by not declaring the extension. Only validate and the explicit check command reach the guard, and validate plans no generation. The guard declares a workspace read, reads only the Git candidate cut and is keyed on `git:**`.

A Git candidate a member project holds under .gen/clientgen or .gen/schema, trees a build owns whole, is a clientgen.committed-generated-contract finding. When an ignore rule excludes it, Git tracks it, and the finding names the git mv to clientgen.json or schema/openapi.json at the project root, or the git rm --cached for a build output; otherwise it asks to ignore .gen and drop any rule that re-includes the file, naming that command only for a tracked copy: the key does not see the index.

Handwritten transport callsites that predate the guard are recorded in a committed census as a count per exact verdict, file, transport and symbol. Censused callsites are reported without failing; anything the census does not account for fails, including a second call of a listed symbol in a listed file. An entry that matches nothing fails, so the census only shrinks, and a malformed census fails instead of being read leniently.

Every detected transport callsite is claimed by an inventory entry or fails. An entry claims exact callsite expressions, never a folder, a file or a transport, and its authority survives an unrelated edit to that file. Only the two generated-binding runtimes may claim `framework-runtime`, every other status is bound to the identity the project manifest declares, and `pending-provider-contract` names the operations it waits on and the work that closes it. No entry silences a first-party reference.

The scanner reads what the source means. A property call such as `this.fetch(sql)` and a method declaration such as `private async fetch(` are not the global transport, and neither is counted. The point where a module takes `globalThis.fetch` or `globalThis.WebSocket` as a value is counted, because that is where a handwritten transport enters the code; a `typeof` capability probe binds nothing and is not.

A project whose putnami.json declares generatedFrom generates its own client from its provider's committed contract through client-generate. No project writes into another, and a consumer reaches a client through its ordinary dependency, so a consumer-only selection generates or restores it. The generation reads the contract its cache key holds: when a provider build in the same session rewrote the contract, it fails rather than store a client under another contract's key.

The @putnami/go and @putnami/typescript build, test, lint, validate, serve and package commands depend on client-generate, so generated code exists before a compiler, a linter or a packager reads it; lint and validate also depend on it across the dependency closure; a project that declares no client-generate plans nothing more.

Git holds no generated client file: the emitters write no client.putnami.json, no client output polices drift, and the check reports a Git candidate carrying the generated-client marker as clientgen.committed-generated-client, naming the git rm --cached and the ignore rule.

api.Clients() and clientGenerator() name no target, output or symbol: they emit the contract's x-putnami-client metadata, each operation's producer project and feature included, into the provider's contract, and no build writes .gen/clientgen/config.json or stages a client.
